State whether each statement is true or false.

spec.description: H is vertically above O. HA, HB and AB are solid; HO, OA and OB are dashed construction lines. The spatial perpendicular marker at O denotes the vertical height, not a right angle between OA and OB.
spec.mathematics: OH=h, AB=5 km, angle HBO=45 degrees, angle HAO=50 degrees. Diagram coordinates specify a schematic projection and are not additional measurements.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens appear; no True/False decisions or derived lengths are shown.

answer.worked: False. $\angle OAB=45^\circ$ from the bearing. In the elevation triangles, $OB=h$ and $OA=h\cot50^\circ<h$, so $\triangle OAB$ is not an isosceles right-angled triangle. In particular, $\angle AOB\ne90^\circ$, so the stated Pythagoras relationship does not hold.
True. From $A$, $O$ is due west and $B$ is south-west. The angle between west and south-west is $45^\circ$.
False. $OB=h$ and $OA=h\cot50^\circ<h$, so $OA<OB$. The angle opposite $OA$ is therefore smaller than the angle opposite $OB$: $\angle OBA<\angle OAB=45^\circ$.

In right-angled $\triangle AOH$,
$$\begin{align*}\tan50^\circ&=\frac{h}{OA}\\OA&=\frac{h}{\tan50^\circ}\\OA&=h\cot50^\circ.\end{align*}$$
True.

In right-angled $\triangle BOH$,
$$\begin{align*}\tan45^\circ&=\frac{h}{OB}\\OB&=h.\end{align*}$$
The included angle between $OA$ and $OB$ is $\angle AOB$, whereas the given $45^\circ$ horizontal angle is $\angle OAB$. The cosine rule gives
$$AB^2=OA^2+OB^2-2(OA)(OB)\cos\angle AOB.$$
False.

Using $OB=h$, $OA=h\cot50^\circ$ and $\angle OAB=45^\circ$, apply the cosine rule in $\triangle OAB$:
$$\begin{align*}OB^2&=AB^2+OA^2-2(AB)(OA)\cos\angle OAB\\h^2&=5^2+(h\cot50^\circ)^2-2(5)(h\cot50^\circ)\cos45^\circ\\h^2&=5^2+(h\cot50^\circ)^2-10h\cot50^\circ\cos45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
True.

answer.short:
$OB=\sqrt{41}\,\mathrm{cm}$, $BX=4.5\,\mathrm{cm}$, $OX=\dfrac{7\sqrt5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}$.

$\angle OBX=90^\circ$, $\angle BOX=35.1^\circ$, $\angle OXB=54.9^\circ$. See the labelled triangle.
answer.worked:
The rectangular base gives $CB=OA=5\,\mathrm{cm}$, and $BX=CY=4.5\,\mathrm{cm}$.

By Pythagoras in $\triangle OCB$,
$$\begin{align*}OB^2&=OC^2+CB^2\\OB^2&=4^2+5^2\\OB^2&=41\\OB&=\sqrt{41}\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$
Since $BX$ is perpendicular to the base, $\angle OBX=90^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}OX^2&=OB^2+BX^2\\OX^2&=41+4.5^2\\OX^2&=\frac{245}{4}\\OX&=\frac{7\sqrt5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\tan\angle BOX&=\frac{BX}{OB}\\\tan\angle BOX&=\frac{4.5}{\sqrt{41}}\\\angle BOX&\approx35.1^\circ\\\angle OXB&=90^\circ-\angle BOX\\\angle OXB&\approx54.9^\circ.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Since $XYZW$ is a rectangle, Pythagoras gives
$$\begin{align*}XZ^2&=XY^2+YZ^2\\XZ^2&=4^2+3^2\\XZ&=5\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$
The angle of elevation is $\theta=\angle SXZ$, between $XS$ and its horizontal projection $XZ$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{ZS}{XZ}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{2}{5}\\\theta&\approx21.8^\circ.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Unshaded square-based pyramid with H above centre O. HA, HB, HC, AB and BC are solid; AD, DC and HD are dashed. The interior altitude HO is dashed. All four base edges have matching single equality ticks.
spec.mathematics: AB=BC=CD=DA=10 cm and AH=8 cm. The right pyramid has O at the centre of ABCD and HO perpendicular to its base. M and P are introduced only in the prompts and are not plotted.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated lengths, requested angles, M or P appear.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The height of $H$ above the square base $ABCD$.

answer.worked:
$O$ is the midpoint of the base diagonal $AC$. In the base and then in right triangle $AOH$:
$$\begin{align*}AC^2&=10^2+10^2\\AC&=10\sqrt2\text{ cm}\\AO&=\frac{10\sqrt2}{2}=5\sqrt2\text{ cm}\\OH^2&=AH^2-AO^2\\OH^2&=8^2-(5\sqrt2)^2=14\\OH&=\sqrt{14}\text{ cm}\approx3.7\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

In right triangle $AOH$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle OAH&=\frac{AO}{AH}\\\cos\angle OAH&=\frac{5\sqrt2}{8}\\\angle OAH&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{5\sqrt2}{8}\right)\approx27.9^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Find $\angle OMH$.

answer.worked:
$OM=5\text{ cm}$ because $O$ is the centre of the square and $M$ is the midpoint of a side. In right triangle $MOH$:
$$\begin{align*}OM&=\frac{10}{2}=5\text{ cm}\\\tan\angle OMH&=\frac{OH}{OM}\\\tan\angle OMH&=\frac{\sqrt{14}}{5}\\\angle OMH&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{14}}{5}\right)\approx36.8^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Let $P$ be a point on $AH$ such that $\angle APB=\angle APD=90^\circ$. Find $\angle BPD$.

inlines.text: , then use the cosine rule in

answer.worked:
The equal slant edges give $BH=DH=AH=8\text{ cm}$. Use the cosine rule in $ABH$ to find the angle shared by $ABH$ and right triangle $ABP$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle BAH&=\frac{AB^2+AH^2-BH^2}{2(AB)(AH)}\\\cos\angle BAH&=\frac{10^2+8^2-8^2}{2(10)(8)}=\frac58\\AP&=AB\cos\angle BAH\\AP&=10\times\frac58=\frac{25}{4}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
Right triangles $ABP$ and $ADP$ have equal hypotenuses and share $AP$, so $PB=PD$. By Pythagoras:
$$\begin{align*}PB^2&=AB^2-AP^2\\PB^2&=10^2-\left(\frac{25}{4}\right)^2=\frac{975}{16}\\PB&=PD=\frac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\text{ cm}\\BD&=10\sqrt2\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
Use the cosine rule in $BPD$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle BPD&=\frac{PB^2+PD^2-BD^2}{2(PB)(PD)}\\\cos\angle BPD&=\frac{\frac{975}{16}+\frac{975}{16}-(10\sqrt2)^2}{2\times\frac{975}{16}}=-\frac{25}{39}\\\angle BPD&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac{25}{39}\right)\approx129.9^\circ\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:

answer.short:

content.prompt:
The diagram shows a wedge with angles marked $\angle XOY=\alpha$, $\angle COY=\beta$ and $\angle BOX=\theta$.

Show that $\sin\theta=\cos\alpha\sin\beta$.

spec.description: Wedge with triangular end faces OCY and ABX, dashed base edges CB and BA, and solid construction segments OX, OB and BX. Three adjacent angle sectors at O identify beta, alpha and theta. Right-angle marks are at C and B.
spec.mathematics: The end faces are congruent, so CY=BX. Triangles OCY and OBX are right-angled at C and B. The longitudinal edge YX is perpendicular to the end face OCY, so triangle OYX is right-angled at Y. The explicit wedge vertices and projection are recorded in the editable code. BX is retained as a solid height construction over its hidden-edge stroke.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source-supplied vertices, edges, construction segments, right-angle markers and angles are visible. No proof or additional answer labels are supplied.

answer.short:
$\displaystyle \cos\alpha\sin\beta=\frac{OY}{OX}\frac{CY}{OY}=\frac{BX}{OX}=\sin\theta$.

Use the equal wedge heights $CY=BX$ and right-angle ratios in $\triangle OYX$, $\triangle OCY$ and $\triangle OBX$.
answer.worked:
The wedge has equal heights $CY=BX$. Also, $YX$ is perpendicular to the end face $OCY$, so $\triangle OYX$ is right-angled at $Y$.

In the three right-angled triangles,
$$\begin{align*}
\cos\alpha&=\frac{OY}{OX}\\
\sin\beta&=\frac{CY}{OY}\\
\sin\theta&=\frac{BX}{OX}.
\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}
\cos\alpha\sin\beta&=\frac{OY}{OX}\times\frac{CY}{OY}\\
\cos\alpha\sin\beta&=\frac{CY}{OX}\\
\cos\alpha\sin\beta&=\frac{BX}{OX}\\
\cos\alpha\sin\beta&=\sin\theta.
\end{align*}$$

Let $P$ and $Q$ be adjacent attachment points, $C$ the ring centre and $S$ the suspension point. Symmetry gives:
$$\begin{align*}\angle PCQ&=\frac{360^\circ}{5}\\\angle PCQ&=72^\circ\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Use Pythagoras to find the equal face altitudes OM and MB, then apply the cosine rule in triangle OMB.

answer.worked:
Let each tetrahedron edge have length $s$, and let $\theta=\angle OMB$. Faces $OAC$ and $BAC$ are equilateral, so their medians $OM$ and $BM$ are perpendicular to $AC$ and have equal lengths.

By Pythagoras in $\triangle OMA$:
$$\begin{align*}OM^2&=s^2-\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^2\\OM^2&=\frac{3s^2}{4}\\OM&=\frac{\sqrt3\,s}{2}.\end{align*}$$
Similarly, $MB=\dfrac{\sqrt3\,s}{2}$, while $OB=s$.

By the cosine rule in $\triangle OMB$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{OM^2+MB^2-OB^2}{2(OM)(MB)}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{\frac{3s^2}{4}+\frac{3s^2}{4}-s^2}{2\left(\frac{\sqrt3\,s}{2}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt3\,s}{2}\right)}\\\cos\theta&=\frac13\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac13\right)\\\theta&\approx70.5^\circ.\end{align*}$$

$\angle AXB=65.28^\circ$.

Find $XA=XB$ from the perpendicular triangles, then use the cosine rule in $\triangle AXB$.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle OCA$, use the cosine rule:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle OCA&=\frac{8^2+6^2-8^2}{2\times8\times6}\\\cos\angle OCA&=\frac38.\end{align*}$$
Since $X$ lies on $OC$ and $AX\perp OC$,
$$\begin{align*}CX&=6\cos\angle OCA\\CX&=\frac94\text{ cm}\\OX&=8-\frac94\\OX&=\frac{23}{4}\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
The right triangles $OXA$ and $OXB$ have equal hypotenuses and share $OX$, so $XA=XB$. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{align*}XA^2&=8^2-\left(\frac{23}{4}\right)^2\\XA^2&=\frac{495}{16}\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle AXB$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle AXB&=\frac{XA^2+XB^2-AB^2}{2(XA)(XB)}\\\cos\angle AXB&=\frac{2\left(\frac{495}{16}\right)-36}{2\left(\frac{495}{16}\right)}\\\cos\angle AXB&=\frac{23}{55}\\\angle AXB&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{23}{55}\right)\\\angle AXB&\approx65.28^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the angle of elevation of $C$ from $A$, correct to two decimal places.

answer.short:
$51.07^\circ$ using the stated $65^\circ$ elevation.

Find the frustum height and the horizontal tangent length, then use the tangent ratio.
answer.worked:
Using the stated elevation of $65^\circ$, let $h$ be the frustum height, $O$ the lower-circle centre, $E$ the vertical projection of $B$, and $D$ the vertical projection of $C$.

$AE=6-3=3\text{ cm}$. The extreme-view point gives a tangent $AD$, so $OD\perp AD$.

$$\begin{align*}
\tan65^\circ&=\frac{h}{3}\\
h&=3\tan65^\circ\\
AD^2&=AO^2-OD^2\\
AD^2&=6^2-3^2\\
AD&=3\sqrt3\text{ cm}\\
\tan\theta&=\frac{3\tan65^\circ}{3\sqrt3}\\
\theta&=51.07^\circ
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the area of $\triangle ABC$, correct to two decimal places.

answer.short:
$10.41\text{ cm}^2$ using the stated $65^\circ$ elevation.

Find the triangle's sides, then use the cosine rule and $\tfrac12 ab\sin C$.
answer.worked:
Using the stated elevation of $65^\circ$, retain $h=3\tan65^\circ$ without rounding. Let $U$ be the upper-circle centre. In the horizontal projection, $\cos\angle BUC=\frac{3}{6}$, so $\angle BUC=60^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}
AB&=\frac{3}{\cos65^\circ}\\
AC^2&=27+h^2\\
BC^2&=3^2+3^2-2(3)(3)\cos60^\circ\\
BC&=3\text{ cm}\\
\cos\angle ABC&=\frac{AB^2+BC^2-AC^2}{2(AB)(BC)}\\
\cos\angle ABC&=\frac{(9+h^2)+9-(27+h^2)}{6AB}\\
\cos\angle ABC&=-\frac{3}{2AB}\\
\operatorname{Area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac12(AB)(3)\sqrt{1-\frac{9}{4AB^2}}\\
\operatorname{Area}(\triangle ABC)&=\frac32\sqrt{\frac{9}{\cos^2 65^\circ}-\frac94}\\
\operatorname{Area}(\triangle ABC)&=10.41\text{ cm}^2
\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Express both ground distances in terms of the height using tangent, then apply the cosine rule.

answer.worked:
Let $O$ be the foot of the tower, with $OA=a$ and $OB=b$. From the two right-angled triangles:
$$\begin{align*}\tan37^\circ&=\frac{h}{a}\\a&=\frac{h}{\tan37^\circ}\\\tan31^\circ&=\frac{h}{b}\\b&=\frac{h}{\tan31^\circ}\end{align*}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle AOB$:
$$\begin{align*}47^2&=\left(\frac{h}{\tan37^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\frac{h}{\tan31^\circ}\right)^2-\frac{2h^2\cos110^\circ}{\tan37^\circ\tan31^\circ}\\h^2&=\frac{47^2}{\frac{1}{\tan^237^\circ}+\frac{1}{\tan^231^\circ}-\frac{2\cos110^\circ}{\tan37^\circ\tan31^\circ}}\\h&=\frac{47}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\tan^237^\circ}+\frac{1}{\tan^231^\circ}-\frac{2\cos110^\circ}{\tan37^\circ\tan31^\circ}}}\\h&\approx19.12\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the angle of elevation of $Q$ from $O$, correct to two decimal places.

inlines.text: Find OA using tangent, OB using the sine rule, then the elevation using tangent.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle OAP$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan37^\circ&=\frac{300}{OA}\\OA&=\frac{300}{\tan37^\circ}.\end{align*}$$
In the ground triangle:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=180^\circ-50^\circ-42^\circ\\\angle AOB&=88^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Using the sine rule in $\triangle OAB$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{OB}{\sin50^\circ}&=\frac{OA}{\sin42^\circ}\\OB&=\frac{300\sin50^\circ}{\tan37^\circ\sin42^\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Let the angle of elevation of $Q$ from $O$ be $\phi$. Since $QB=300\text{ m}$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\phi&=\frac{300}{OB}\\\phi&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\tan37^\circ\sin42^\circ}{\sin50^\circ}\right)\\\phi&\approx33.35^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the distance the helicopter flew from $P$ to $Q$, correct to two decimal places.

inlines.text: Use the sine rule to find AB; the equal flight heights give PQ = AB.

answer.worked:
Using $OA=\dfrac{300}{\tan37^\circ}$ from part (a), in $\triangle OAB$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle AOB&=180^\circ-50^\circ-42^\circ\\\angle AOB&=88^\circ\\\frac{AB}{\sin88^\circ}&=\frac{OA}{\sin42^\circ}\\AB&=\frac{300\sin88^\circ}{\tan37^\circ\sin42^\circ}.\end{align*}$$
The helicopter maintains the same vertical height, so its flight distance equals the ground separation:
$$\begin{align*}PQ&=AB\\PQ&\approx594.61\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Use the sine rule in the horizontal triangle, then find the perpendicular distance to the road and apply the elevation angle.

answer.worked:
Let $P$ and $O$ be Mary's starting and final positions, $M$ the mountain's base, $A$ the closest point on the road and $H$ the summit. The reverse bearing from $O$ to $P$ is $135^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle MPO&=335^\circ-315^\circ=20^\circ\\\angle POM&=135^\circ-105^\circ=30^\circ\\\angle PMO&=180^\circ-20^\circ-30^\circ=130^\circ\end{align*}$$

Apply the sine rule in $\triangle POM$:

$$\begin{align*}\frac{PM}{\sin30^\circ}&=\frac{142}{\sin130^\circ}\\PM&=\frac{142\sin30^\circ}{\sin130^\circ}\end{align*}$$

Since $AM$ is perpendicular to the road, $\triangle PAM$ is right-angled. Using the unrounded value of $PM$,

$$\begin{align*}AM&=\frac{142\sin30^\circ}{\sin130^\circ}\sin20^\circ\end{align*}$$

In right-angled $\triangle AMH$,

$$\begin{align*}\tan8^\circ&=\frac{MH}{AM}\\MH&=\frac{142\sin30^\circ\sin20^\circ}{\sin130^\circ}\tan8^\circ\\MH&\approx4.455\text{ km}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the distance $WT$. Give your answer in metres, correct to two decimal places.

answer.short:
$645.97\text{ m}$

Use tangent to find the horizontal distances, then the cosine rule with included angle $85^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Let $B$ denote Bob's position, $d_T=BT$ and $d_W=BW$. The angle between the ground directions is $210^\circ-125^\circ=85^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\tan35^\circ&=\frac{140}{d_T}\\d_T&=\frac{140}{\tan35^\circ}\\\tan20^\circ&=\frac{230}{d_W}\\d_W&=\frac{230}{\tan20^\circ}\\WT^2&=d_T^2+d_W^2-2d_Td_W\cos85^\circ\\WT^2&=\left(\frac{140}{\tan35^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\frac{230}{\tan20^\circ}\right)^2-2\left(\frac{140}{\tan35^\circ}\right)\left(\frac{230}{\tan20^\circ}\right)\cos85^\circ\\WT&\approx645.97\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the angle between the top of the wind turbine, Bob, and the top of the tower. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

answer.short:
$74.74^\circ$

Find the two sight-line lengths and the distance between the tops, then apply the cosine rule.
answer.worked:
Let $U$ be the top of the tower, $V$ the top of the wind turbine and $B$ Bob's position. The tops differ in height by $230-140=90\text{ m}$. Use the unrounded value of $WT$ from part (a).

$$\begin{align*}\sin35^\circ&=\frac{140}{BU}\\BU&=\frac{140}{\sin35^\circ}\\\sin20^\circ&=\frac{230}{BV}\\BV&=\frac{230}{\sin20^\circ}\\UV^2&=WT^2+90^2\\\cos\angle UBV&=\frac{BU^2+BV^2-UV^2}{2(BU)(BV)}\\\cos\angle UBV&=\frac{\left(\frac{140}{\sin35^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\frac{230}{\sin20^\circ}\right)^2-(WT^2+90^2)}{2\left(\frac{140}{\sin35^\circ}\right)\left(\frac{230}{\sin20^\circ}\right)}\\\angle UBV&\approx74.74^\circ\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
An observer from point $A$ sees the top of a pole with an angle of elevation $30^\circ$. After walking $5\text{ m}$ the angle of elevation is now $45^\circ$. After another $8\text{ m}$, the angle of elevation is $60^\circ$.

Find the height of the pole, correct to one decimal place.

spec.description: Pole OH with three sight lines, collinear route C–B–A, successive distances 8 m and 5 m, and elevation angles 60°, 45° and 30°.
spec.mathematics: C, B and A are collinear in that order; CB:BA=8:5. OH is perpendicular to the horizontal ground plane. HC, HB and HA are solid sight lines; OC, OB, OA and OH retain the source dashed construction style. Screen coordinates describe an illustrative projection, not additional numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: All labels are supplied givens; no calculated height is visible.

inlines.text: Express the ground distances using tangent, then eliminate the supplementary ground angles with the cosine rule.

answer.worked:
Let $OH=h$ metres and $\theta=\angle OBC$. From the three right-angled triangles,
$$\begin{align*}OA&=\frac{h}{\tan30^\circ}=\sqrt3h\\OB&=\frac{h}{\tan45^\circ}=h\\OC&=\frac{h}{\tan60^\circ}=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}.\end{align*}$$
Since $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear, $\angle OBA=180^\circ-\theta$. Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle OBA$:
$$\begin{align*}OA^2&=OB^2+BA^2-2(OB)(BA)\cos(180^\circ-\theta)\\3h^2&=h^2+25+10h\cos\theta\\10h\cos\theta&=2h^2-25.\end{align*}$$
In $\triangle OBC$:
$$\begin{align*}OC^2&=OB^2+BC^2-2(OB)(BC)\cos\theta\\\frac{h^2}{3}&=h^2+64-16h\cos\theta\\16h\cos\theta&=\frac{2h^2}{3}+64.\end{align*}$$
Eliminate $h\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}16(2h^2-25)&=10\left(\frac{2h^2}{3}+64\right)\\\frac{76h^2}{3}&=1040\\h^2&=\frac{780}{19}\\h&=\sqrt{\frac{780}{19}}\text{ m}\\h&\approx6.4\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: by the cosine rule, obtain its sine using a right triangle, then use the triangle area formula.

answer.worked:
Let $OP=x$, $OQ=y$, $OR=z$ and $\theta=\angle PRQ$. The perpendicular faces give
$$\begin{align*}A_1&=\frac{xy}{2}\\A_2&=\frac{xz}{2}\\A_3&=\frac{yz}{2}.\end{align*}$$
By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}PR^2&=x^2+z^2\\QR^2&=y^2+z^2\\PQ^2&=x^2+y^2.\end{align*}$$
Write $D=\sqrt{(x^2+z^2)(y^2+z^2)}$ and $S=x^2y^2+x^2z^2+y^2z^2$. By the cosine rule,
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{PR^2+QR^2-PQ^2}{2(PR)(QR)}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{(x^2+z^2)+(y^2+z^2)-(x^2+y^2)}{2D}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{z^2}{D}.\end{align*}$$
In the auxiliary right triangle, the hypotenuse is $D$ and the side adjacent to $\theta$ is $z^2$. Its opposite side is
$$\begin{align*}\sqrt{D^2-z^4}&=\sqrt{(x^2+z^2)(y^2+z^2)-z^4}\\\sqrt{D^2-z^4}&=\sqrt S.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\sin\theta=\sqrt S/D$. The area of $\triangle PQR$ is
$$\begin{align*}A_4&=\frac12(PR)(QR)\sin\theta\\A_4&=\frac12D\frac{\sqrt S}{D}\\A_4&=\frac{\sqrt S}{2}\\A_4^2&=\frac{x^2y^2+x^2z^2+y^2z^2}{4}\\A_4^2&=A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Express the ground distances using tangent, then apply the cosine rule in triangles OBC and OBA, using the supplementary angles at B.

answer.worked:
From the three right-angled elevation triangles,
$$\begin{align*}
OA&=\frac{h}{\tan45^\circ}=h\\
OB&=\frac{h}{\tan60^\circ}=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}\\
OC&=\frac{h}{\tan30^\circ}=\sqrt3h.
\end{align*}$$
Let $\theta=\angle OBC$. Since $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear, $\angle OBA=180^\circ-\theta$ and $\cos\angle OBA=-\cos\theta$.

Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle OBC$:
$$\begin{align*}
3h^2&=\frac{h^2}{3}+b^2-\frac{2bh}{\sqrt3}\cos\theta\\
\frac{2bh}{\sqrt3}\cos\theta&=b^2-\frac{8h^2}{3}.
\end{align*}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle OBA$ and substitute:
$$\begin{align*}
h^2&=\frac{h^2}{3}+a^2+\frac{2ah}{\sqrt3}\cos\theta\\
h^2&=\frac{h^2}{3}+a^2+\frac{a}{b}\left(b^2-\frac{8h^2}{3}\right)\\
h^2\left(\frac23+\frac{8a}{3b}\right)&=a(a+b)\\
h^2&=\frac{3ab(a+b)}{2(4a+b)}\\
h&=\sqrt{\frac{3ab(a+b)}{2(4a+b)}}.
\end{align*}$$
The positive square root is taken because $h$ is a height.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find $\cos\angle ACB$ in terms of $d$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\theta$.

answer.short:
$\displaystyle\cos\angle ACB=\frac{\cos^2\beta\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\theta-\cos^2\alpha\cos^2\beta}{2\cos\theta\sin\theta\cos\alpha\cos\beta}$.

Express $AC$ and $BC$ using the right-angled triangles, then apply the cosine rule in $\triangle ACB$; $d$ cancels.
answer.worked:
From the right-angled triangles $OAB$, $OAC$ and $OBC$:
$$\begin{align*}OA&=d\cos\theta\\OB&=d\sin\theta\\AC&=\frac{OA}{\cos\alpha}\\AC&=\frac{d\cos\theta}{\cos\alpha}\\BC&=\frac{OB}{\cos\beta}\\BC&=\frac{d\sin\theta}{\cos\beta}.\end{align*}$$
By the cosine rule in $\triangle ACB$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{AC^2+BC^2-AB^2}{2(AC)(BC)}\\\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{\dfrac{d^2\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\alpha}+\dfrac{d^2\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\beta}-d^2}{\dfrac{2d^2\cos\theta\sin\theta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}}\\\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{\cos^2\beta\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\theta-\cos^2\alpha\cos^2\beta}{2\cos\theta\sin\theta\cos\alpha\cos\beta}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $$\cos\angle ACB=\frac{\tan\theta}{2},$$ given the condition that $\alpha=\beta=\theta$.

answer.short:
$\displaystyle\cos\angle ACB=\frac{\tan\theta}{2}$.

Substitute $\alpha=\beta=\theta$ into part (a) and use $1-\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta$.
answer.worked:
Substitute $\alpha=\beta=\theta$ into part (a):
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{\cos^4\theta+\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta-\cos^4\theta}{2\cos^3\theta\sin\theta}\\\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta}{2\cos^3\theta\sin\theta}\\\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{\sin\theta}{2\cos\theta}\\\cos\angle ACB&=\frac{\tan\theta}{2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Deduce that if also $\angle ACB=60^\circ$, then $\triangle ACB$ is an equilateral triangle.

answer.short:
$\alpha=\beta=\theta=45^\circ$, so $OA=OB=OC$ and $AC=BC=AB=d$. Hence $\triangle ACB$ is equilateral.

Use part (b), then the three isosceles right-angled component triangles.
answer.worked:
Using part (b):
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=2\cos60^\circ\\\tan\theta&=1\\\theta&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\alpha=\beta=\theta=45^\circ$. The right-angled triangle $OAB$ gives $OA=OB$, triangle $OAC$ gives $OA=OC$, and triangle $OBC$ gives $OB=OC$. Therefore $OA=OB=OC$, and
$$\begin{align*}AB^2&=OA^2+OB^2=2OA^2\\AC^2&=OA^2+OC^2=2OA^2\\BC^2&=OB^2+OC^2=2OA^2.\end{align*}$$
Hence $AC=BC=AB=d$, so $\triangle ACB$ is equilateral.

answer.short:
$\displaystyle\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac13\right)\approx109.5^\circ$.

Use regular-tetrahedron symmetry to find the equal bond lengths, then apply the cosine rule to the triangle formed by two bonds.
answer.worked:
Let the tetrahedron have edge length $a$. Let $V$ be its top vertex, $M$ the centre of the opposite equilateral face, $O$ the carbon atom and $H$ a vertex of that face. Write $VM=h$ and $OV=OH=r$.

In the equilateral base, $MH=a/\sqrt3$. Since $VM$ is perpendicular to the base, Pythagoras gives
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=a^2-\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt3}\right)^2\\h^2&=\frac{2a^2}{3}.\end{align*}$$
By symmetry, $O$ lies on $VM$, so $OM=h-r$. In right-angled $\triangle OMH$:
$$\begin{align*}r^2&=(h-r)^2+\frac{a^2}{3}\\2hr&=h^2+\frac{a^2}{3}\\2hr&=a^2\\r^2&=\frac{a^4}{4h^2}\\r^2&=\frac{3a^2}{8}.\end{align*}$$
For the bond angle $\phi=\angle VOH$, the cosine rule in $\triangle VOH$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\cos\phi&=\frac{r^2+r^2-a^2}{2r^2}\\\cos\phi&=\frac{\frac{3a^2}{4}-a^2}{\frac{3a^2}{4}}\\\cos\phi&=-\frac13\\\phi&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac13\right)\\\phi&\approx109.5^\circ.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Use the sine rule and equal angles subtended by chord BC to obtain
; then apply the cosine rule in

answer.worked:
Angles subtended by chord $BC$ are equal, so $\angle BDC=\angle BAC$. The sine rule in $\triangle BCD$ gives
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{BD}{\sin\theta}&=\frac{BC}{\sin\angle BDC}\\
\frac{BD}{\sin\theta}&=\frac{BC}{\sin\angle BAC}\\
\frac{BD}{\sin\theta}&=AC.
\end{align*}$$
The last equality uses $\sin\angle BAC=BC/AC$ in right-angled $\triangle ABC$. Hence
$$AC^2=\frac{BD^2}{\sin^2\theta}.$$
Opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ are supplementary, so $\angle BAD=180^\circ-\theta$. In $\triangle ABD$, the cosine rule gives
$$\begin{align*}
BD^2&=AB^2+AD^2-2(AB)(AD)\cos(180^\circ-\theta)\\
BD^2&=AB^2+AD^2+2(AB)(AD)\cos\theta.
\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}
AC^2&=\frac{BD^2}{\sin^2\theta}\\
AC^2&=\frac{AB^2+AD^2+2(AB)(AD)\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}.
\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Express AC, AB and AD using the common height AH, substitute into part (a), and cancel

answer.worked:
Since $AH$ is perpendicular to the circle's plane, $\triangle HAC$, $\triangle HAB$ and $\triangle HAD$ are right-angled at $A$. Thus
$$\begin{align*}
AC&=AH\cot\varphi,\\
AB&=AH\cot\alpha,\\
AD&=AH\cot\beta.
\end{align*}$$
Substitute into part (a):
$$AH^2\cot^2\varphi=\frac{AH^2\cot^2\alpha+AH^2\cot^2\beta+2AH^2\cos\theta\cot\alpha\cot\beta}{\sin^2\theta}.$$
Cancel $AH^2$:
$$\cot^2\varphi=\frac{\cot^2\alpha+\cot^2\beta+2\cos\theta\cot\alpha\cot\beta}{\sin^2\theta}.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: If $\alpha=45^\circ$, $\beta=60^\circ$ and $\varphi=30^\circ$, find the acute angle $\theta$ correct to one decimal place.

inlines.text: , and select the positive cosine because θ is acute.

answer.worked:
Using $\cot45^\circ=1$, $\cot60^\circ=1/\sqrt3$ and $\cot30^\circ=\sqrt3$, part (b) gives
$$\begin{align*}
3&=\frac{1+\frac13+\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\\
3\sin^2\theta&=\frac43+\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\cos\theta\\
3(1-\cos^2\theta)&=\frac43+\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\cos\theta\\
9\cos^2\theta+2\sqrt3\cos\theta-5&=0\\
(\sqrt3\cos\theta-1)(3\sqrt3\cos\theta+5)&=0.
\end{align*}$$
Since $\theta$ is acute, $\cos\theta>0$, so
$$\begin{align*}
\cos\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt3}\\
\theta&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)\approx54.7^\circ.
\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Find perpendicular face heights using Pythagoras, then use triangle and trapezium area formulas.

answer.worked:
Let $a=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $b=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. The offsets from each end-plane centre are $(\pm a,\pm a)$ for the square and $X=(0,1)$, $Y=(-b,-\frac12)$, $Z=(b,-\frac12)$ for the triangle. Lengths are in centimetres.

The square side is $2a=\sqrt2$ and the equilateral triangle side is $2b=\sqrt3$.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. The height from $X$ to $AB$ is $XM$, since the horizontal offset of $X$ is zero. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}XM^2&=4^2+(1-a)^2\\XM&=\sqrt{16+(1-a)^2}\\|ABX|&=\frac12(2a)\sqrt{16+(1-a)^2}\\|ABX|&\approx2.836\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$

For $BCY$, the perpendicular from $Y$ meets $BC$ at vertical offset $-\frac12$. Its height $h_1$ combines the centre separation and horizontal offset $b-a$:
$$\begin{align*}h_1^2&=4^2+(b-a)^2\\|BCY|=|ADZ|&=\frac12(2a)\sqrt{16+(b-a)^2}\\|BCY|=|ADZ|&\approx2.831\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$

To find the height of $BXY$, project $B$ perpendicularly onto the triangle's end plane at $B'$. In that plane, the line $XY$ makes $60^\circ$ with the horizontal. The perpendicular distance $d$ from $B'$ to $XY$ is
$$\begin{align*}d&=a\sin60^\circ+a\cos60^\circ-\frac12\\d&=a\left(b+\frac12\right)-\frac12.\end{align*}$$
The perpendicular height $h_2$ of $BXY$ follows by Pythagoras:
$$\begin{align*}h_2^2&=4^2+d^2\\|BXY|=|AXZ|&=\frac12(2b)\sqrt{16+\left[a\left(b+\frac12\right)-\frac12\right]^2}\\|BXY|=|AXZ|&\approx3.488\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$

The parallel sides of trapezium $CYZD$ are $CD=2a$ and $YZ=2b$. Its perpendicular height $h_3$ combines the centre separation and vertical offset $a-\frac12$:
$$\begin{align*}h_3^2&=4^2+\left(a-\frac12\right)^2\\|CYZD|&=\frac12(2a+2b)\sqrt{16+\left(a-\frac12\right)^2}\\|CYZD|&\approx6.301\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$

For the two end faces,
$$\begin{align*}|ABCD|&=(\sqrt2)^2\\|ABCD|&=2.000\text{ cm}^2\\|XYZ|&=\frac12(\sqrt3)\left(1+\frac12\right)\\|XYZ|&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\\|XYZ|&\approx1.299\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$A+B=45^\circ$ and $C=45^\circ$, so $A+B+C=90^\circ$.

$$A+B+C=45^\circ+45^\circ=90^\circ.$$

answer.short:
$\tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A\tan B\tan C$.

Use $A+B+C=180^\circ$ and expand the tangent sum twice; its numerator is zero.
answer.worked:
Since $A+B+C=180^\circ$, let $x=\tan A$, $y=\tan B$ and $z=\tan C$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan(A+B+C)&=\frac{\tan(A+B)+z}{1-z\tan(A+B)}\\\tan(A+B+C)&=\frac{\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}+z}{1-z\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}}\\\tan(A+B+C)&=\frac{x+y+z-xyz}{1-xy-xz-yz}\\\tan(A+B+C)&=\tan180^\circ=0.\end{align*}$$
Hence the numerator is zero:
$$\begin{align*}x+y+z&=xyz\\\tan A+\tan B+\tan C&=\tan A\tan B\tan C.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt:
Find $A$, $B$ and $C$ given
$$\tan A:\tan B:\tan C=1:3:-5.$$

answer.short:
$A\approx14^\circ$, $B\approx38^\circ$, $C\approx128^\circ$.

Substitute $\tan A=k$, $\tan B=3k$ and $\tan C=-5k$ into part (a); choose the obtuse angle for $C$.
answer.worked:
Let $\tan A=k$, $\tan B=3k$ and $\tan C=-5k$. The triangle cannot have two obtuse angles, so $k>0$; $A$ and $B$ are acute and $C$ is obtuse.
Using part (a),
$$\begin{align*}k+3k-5k&=k(3k)(-5k)\\-k&=-15k^3\\k^2&=\frac1{15}\\k&=\frac1{\sqrt{15}}.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, to the nearest degree,
$$\begin{align*}A&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac1{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx14^\circ\\B&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac3{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx38^\circ\\C&=180^\circ-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac5{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx128^\circ.\end{align*}$$

Expand $\sin(2x+x)$ using the sum and double-angle identities, then divide by $\sin x$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\sin 3x&=\sin(2x+x)\\\sin 3x&=\sin 2x\cos x+\cos 2x\sin x\\\sin 3x&=2\sin x\cos^2x+(1-2\sin^2x)\sin x\\\sin 3x&=2\sin x(1-\sin^2x)+\sin x-2\sin^3x\\\sin 3x&=3\sin x-4\sin^3x.\end{align*}$$
For $x\ne0,\pi,2\pi$, we have $\sin x\ne0$, so
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{3\sin x-4\sin^3x}{\sin x}\\f(x)&=3-4\sin^2x.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$\tan^2\theta=\dfrac{x-y}{x+y}$.

Use $\tan\theta=h/(x+y)$ and $\tan2\theta=h/y$, then substitute the tangent double-angle identity and rearrange.
answer.worked:
From the two right triangles,
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{h}{x+y}\\\tan2\theta&=\frac{h}{y}.\end{align*}$$
Using the double-angle identity,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}&=\frac{h}{y}\\\frac{2h}{(x+y)(1-\tan^2\theta)}&=\frac{h}{y}\\2y&=(x+y)(1-\tan^2\theta)\\\tan^2\theta&=1-\frac{2y}{x+y}\\\tan^2\theta&=\frac{x-y}{x+y}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A triangle has side-lengths 8, 10 and 12 units. Show that the largest angle is exactly double the smallest angle.

answer.short:
$\alpha=2\beta$, where $\alpha$ is opposite 12 and $\beta$ is opposite 8.

The cosine rule gives $\cos\alpha=1/8$ and $\cos\beta=3/4$, so $\cos2\beta=2(3/4)^2-1=1/8=\cos\alpha$.
answer.worked:
Let $\alpha$ be the largest angle, opposite 12, and $\beta$ the smallest angle, opposite 8. By the cosine rule,
$$\begin{align*}\cos\alpha&=\frac{8^2+10^2-12^2}{2\times8\times10}\\\cos\alpha&=\frac18\\\cos\beta&=\frac{10^2+12^2-8^2}{2\times10\times12}\\\cos\beta&=\frac34.\end{align*}$$
Then
$$\begin{align*}\cos2\beta&=2\cos^2\beta-1\\\cos2\beta&=2\left(\frac34\right)^2-1\\\cos2\beta&=\frac18.\end{align*}$$
Since $\beta$ is acute, both $\alpha$ and $2\beta$ lie between $0$ and $\pi$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on this interval, so $\alpha=2\beta$.

content.prompt:
Let $\triangle ABC$ have side lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$.

Let $P$ and $Q$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $P$ and $Q$ are equidistant from $A$. Suppose that the interval $PQ$ bisects the area of $\triangle ABC$.

Show that $PQ=\sqrt{2bc}\sin\left(\dfrac A2\right)$.

answer.short:
$PQ=\sqrt{2bc}\sin(A/2)$.

Put $AP=AQ=r$. The area condition gives $r^2=bc/2$; the cosine rule then gives $PQ^2=bc(1-\cos A)=2bc\sin^2(A/2)$.
answer.worked:
Let $AP=AQ=r$. Since $AB=c$ and $AC=b$, the area condition gives
$$\begin{align*}\frac12r^2\sin A&=\frac12\left(\frac12bc\sin A\right)\\r^2&=\frac{bc}{2}.\end{align*}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle APQ$:
$$\begin{align*}PQ^2&=r^2+r^2-2r^2\cos A\\PQ^2&=2r^2(1-\cos A)\\PQ^2&=bc(1-\cos A)\\PQ^2&=2bc\sin^2\left(\frac A2\right).\end{align*}$$
Here $1-\cos A=2\sin^2(A/2)$ follows from the cosine double-angle identity. Since $0<A<\pi$, $\sin(A/2)>0$, and hence
$$PQ=\sqrt{2bc}\sin\left(\frac A2\right).$$

content.prompt: Describe the curve $(\sin t+\cos t,\sin2t)$.

answer.short:
The parabola segment $y=x^2-1$ for $-\sqrt2\le x\le\sqrt2$, with vertex $(0,-1)$ and endpoints $(-\sqrt2,1)$ and $(\sqrt2,1)$.

Square $x=\sin t+\cos t$ and use $\sin2t=2\sin t\cos t$.
answer.worked:
Put $x=\sin t+\cos t$ and $y=\sin2t$. Then
$$\begin{align*}x^2&=(\sin t+\cos t)^2\\x^2&=\sin^2t+\cos^2t+2\sin t\cos t\\x^2&=1+\sin2t\\x^2&=1+y.\end{align*}$$
Also, $x=\sqrt2\sin(t+\pi/4)$, so $-\sqrt2\le x\le\sqrt2$, and every value in this interval occurs.

The curve is the segment of $y=x^2-1$ on this interval, with vertex $(0,-1)$ and endpoints $(-\sqrt2,1)$ and $(\sqrt2,1)$.

content.prompt: Let $0\leq\theta\leq2\pi$. Find all values of $\theta$ if $$x^2+4x\sin\theta+\tan\theta=0$$ has equal roots.

answer.short:
$\theta=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{13\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ 2\pi$.

Set the discriminant to zero, then retain both factors of $\sin\theta(4\sin\theta\cos\theta-1)=0$.
answer.worked:
Equal roots require a zero discriminant. Since $\tan\theta$ is defined, $\cos\theta\ne0$.

$$\begin{align*}(4\sin\theta)^2-4\tan\theta&=0\\4\sin^2\theta-\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=0\\4\sin^2\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(4\sin\theta\cos\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$

If $\sin\theta=0$, then $\theta=0,\pi,2\pi$.

For the other factor,

$$\begin{align*}4\sin\theta\cos\theta&=1\\\sin2\theta&=\frac12.\end{align*}$$

Since $0\leq2\theta\leq4\pi$,

$$\begin{align*}2\theta&=\frac\pi6,\ \frac{5\pi}6,\ \frac{13\pi}6,\ \frac{17\pi}6\\\theta&=\frac\pi{12},\ \frac{5\pi}{12},\ \frac{13\pi}{12},\ \frac{17\pi}{12}.\end{align*}$$

All seven values have $\cos\theta\ne0$ and give a zero discriminant. Thus

$$\theta=0,\ \frac\pi{12},\ \frac{5\pi}{12},\ \pi,\ \frac{13\pi}{12},\ \frac{17\pi}{12},\ 2\pi.$$

answer.short:
$\displaystyle \frac yx=\frac{1}{3-4\sin^2\theta}$, so $\displaystyle \frac13<\frac yx<\frac12$.

Use differences of the three horizontal distances and $0<\theta<\pi/6$.
answer.worked:
All three observer positions are before the tower, so $0<3\theta<\pi/2$, giving $0<\theta<\pi/6$.

The horizontal distances from the tower are $h\cot\theta$, $h\cot2\theta$ and $h\cot3\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}x&=h(\cot\theta-\cot2\theta)\\x&=h\frac{\cos\theta\sin2\theta-\cos2\theta\sin\theta}{\sin\theta\sin2\theta}\\x&=h\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin\theta\sin2\theta}\\x&=\frac h{\sin2\theta},\\y&=h(\cot2\theta-\cot3\theta)\\y&=h\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin2\theta\sin3\theta},\\\frac yx&=\frac{\sin\theta}{\sin3\theta}.\end{align*}$$

Using the sum and double-angle identities,

$$\begin{align*}\sin3\theta&=\sin2\theta\cos\theta+\cos2\theta\sin\theta\\\sin3\theta&=2\sin\theta\cos^2\theta+(1-2\sin^2\theta)\sin\theta\\\sin3\theta&=\sin\theta(3-4\sin^2\theta),\\\frac yx&=\frac1{3-4\sin^2\theta}.\end{align*}$$

Since $0<\theta<\pi/6$, we have $0<\sin^2\theta<1/4$. Thus $2<3-4\sin^2\theta<3$, and consequently

$$\frac13<\frac yx<\frac12.$$

Therefore $x/3<y<x/2$.

answer.short:
$$\begin{aligned}&\sec\theta+\sec2\theta+\sec4\theta\\
&=\frac12\Big[\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\theta2\right)\\
&\quad+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\theta2\right)\\
&\quad+\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\theta\right)+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)\\
&\quad+\tan\left(\frac\pi4+2\theta\right)+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-2\theta\right)\Big].\end{aligned}$$

Add part (a) for opposite signs of the angle, then apply the result to $\theta$, $2\theta$ and $4\theta$.
answer.worked:
Part (a), with $\theta$ and $-\theta$, gives

$$\begin{align*}\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\theta2\right)&=\sec\theta+\tan\theta,\\\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\theta2\right)&=\sec\theta-\tan\theta.\end{align*}$$

Adding,

$$\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\theta2\right)+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\theta2\right)=2\sec\theta.$$

Therefore

$$\sec\theta=\frac12\left(\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\theta2\right)+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\theta2\right)\right).$$

Apply this identity to $\theta$, $2\theta$ and $4\theta$:

$$\begin{aligned}\sec\theta+\sec2\theta+\sec4\theta
&=\frac12\Bigg[\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\theta2\right)+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\theta2\right)\\
&\qquad+\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\theta\right)+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)\\
&\qquad+\tan\left(\frac\pi4+2\theta\right)+\tan\left(\frac\pi4-2\theta\right)\Bigg].\end{aligned}$$

answer.worked:
Let $t=\tan\theta$. Using the double-angle and sum identities,
$$\begin{align*}\tan2\theta&=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}\\\tan3\theta&=\frac{\tan2\theta+t}{1-t\tan2\theta}\\\tan3\theta&=\frac{\frac{2t}{1-t^2}+t}{1-\frac{2t^2}{1-t^2}}\\\tan3\theta&=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}.\end{align*}$$
The given product therefore gives
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2t(3t-t^3)}{(1-t^2)(1-3t^2)}&=1\\6t^2-2t^4&=1-4t^2+3t^4\\5t^4-10t^2+1&=0\\5\tan^4\theta-10\tan^2\theta+1&=0.\end{align*}$$

Let $u=\tan^2 18^\circ$. By part (a),

content.prompt: Typically, the condition on $R$ is that it must be positive. What happens if it’s negative?

answer.short:
Absorb the minus sign into the auxiliary angle: replace $R$ by $|R|$ and shift the angle by $\pi$.

For example, $R\cos(x-\alpha)=|R|\cos\bigl(x-(\alpha+\pi)\bigr)$ when $R<0$.
answer.worked:
If $R<0$, then $R=-|R|$. For a cosine-difference form,
$$\begin{align*}R\cos(x-\alpha)&=-|R|\cos(x-\alpha)\\R\cos(x-\alpha)&=|R|\cos\bigl(x-(\alpha+\pi)\bigr).\end{align*}$$
A phase shift of $\pi$ reverses the sign of either sine or cosine. Hence we conventionally use $R>0$ and absorb the minus sign into the auxiliary angle.

children.prompt: Express $4\cos\theta+3\sin\theta$ in the form $R\cos(\theta-\alpha)$ where $R>0$ and $0^\circ\le\alpha\le360^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Equating coefficients gives
$$\begin{align*}R\cos\alpha&=4\\R\sin\alpha&=3\\R&=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5\\\tan\alpha&=\frac34.\end{align*}$$
Since $\cos\alpha>0$ and $\sin\alpha>0$, $\alpha$ is in the first quadrant. Hence $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac34\right)$ and
$$4\cos\theta+3\sin\theta=5\cos\!\left(\theta-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac34\right)\right).$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: The prescribed cosine-difference form matches the coefficient procedure on page 33; retain an exact auxiliary angle.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, solve $4\cos\theta+3\sin\theta=1$ for $0\le\theta\le360^\circ$. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

answer.short:
$\theta=115^\circ,\ 318^\circ$.

Use the transformation from part a and solve over the shifted interval.
answer.worked:
Using $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac34\right)$ from part a,
$$\begin{align*}5\cos(\theta-\alpha)&=1\\\cos(\theta-\alpha)&=\frac15.\end{align*}$$
The shifted interval is $-\alpha\le\theta-\alpha\le360^\circ-\alpha$. Let $\beta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac15\right)$. The two angles in this interval are $\beta$ and $360^\circ-\beta$.
$$\begin{align*}\theta-\alpha&=\beta,\ 360^\circ-\beta\\\theta&=\alpha+\beta,\ \alpha+360^\circ-\beta\\\theta&\approx115.33294^\circ,\ 318.40686^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\theta=115^\circ,\ 318^\circ$, to the nearest degree.

$R=\sqrt{2+2\cos\beta}$.

Expand the shifted cosine and use $R^2=(1+\cos\beta)^2+\sin^2\beta$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\cos x+\cos x\cos\beta-\sin x\sin\beta\\f(x)&=(1+\cos\beta)\cos x-\sin\beta\sin x.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, find the values of $\beta$ that give the largest and smallest possible amplitudes of $f$.

answer.short: Largest amplitude: $2$ at $\beta=0$; smallest amplitude: $\sqrt2$ at $\beta=\frac\pi2$.

$$\begin{align*}R(0)&=\sqrt{2+2}=2\\R\left(\frac\pi2\right)&=\sqrt{2+0}=\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
Thus the largest amplitude occurs at $\beta=0$ and the smallest at $\beta=\frac\pi2$.

content.prompt: Given $\cos(\theta+\alpha)=p$ and $\sin(\theta+\beta)=q$. Assume $\cos(\alpha-\beta)\ne0$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Express $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ in terms of $\alpha,\beta,p$ and $q$.

answer.short:
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{p\cos\beta+q\sin\alpha}{\cos(\alpha-\beta)}$, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{q\cos\alpha-p\sin\beta}{\cos(\alpha-\beta)}$.

Expand the givens and eliminate each unknown in turn.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}p&=\cos\theta\cos\alpha-\sin\theta\sin\alpha\\q&=\sin\theta\cos\beta+\cos\theta\sin\beta.\end{align*}$$
Multiply the first equation by $\cos\beta$ and the second by $\sin\alpha$, then add:
$$\begin{align*}p\cos\beta+q\sin\alpha&=\cos\theta(\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta)\\p\cos\beta+q\sin\alpha&=\cos\theta\cos(\alpha-\beta)\\\cos\theta&=\frac{p\cos\beta+q\sin\alpha}{\cos(\alpha-\beta)}.\end{align*}$$
Multiply the second equation by $\cos\alpha$ and subtract the first multiplied by $\sin\beta$:
$$\begin{align*}q\cos\alpha-p\sin\beta&=\sin\theta(\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta)\\q\cos\alpha-p\sin\beta&=\sin\theta\cos(\alpha-\beta)\\\sin\theta&=\frac{q\cos\alpha-p\sin\beta}{\cos(\alpha-\beta)}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$p^2+q^2+2pq\sin(\alpha-\beta)=\cos^2(\alpha-\beta)$.

Substitute part (a) into $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ and simplify the mixed term.
answer.worked:
Substitute part (a) into $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ and multiply by $\cos^2(\alpha-\beta)$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos^2(\alpha-\beta)&=(p\cos\beta+q\sin\alpha)^2+(q\cos\alpha-p\sin\beta)^2\\\cos^2(\alpha-\beta)&=p^2(\cos^2\beta+\sin^2\beta)+q^2(\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha)\\&\quad+2pq(\sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta)\\\cos^2(\alpha-\beta)&=p^2+q^2+2pq\sin(\alpha-\beta).\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Solving $\tan 2x=\cot x$ has the same solutions as $$\tan^2x=\frac13.$$

answer.short: False. The original equation also has solutions with $\cos x=0$, where $\tan x$ is undefined.

For example, at $x=90^\circ$,

$$\begin{align*}\tan(2\times90^\circ)&=\tan180^\circ\\\tan(2\times90^\circ)&=0\\\cot90^\circ&=0\end{align*}$$

Thus $90^\circ$ satisfies the original equation, but $\tan^2 90^\circ$ is undefined. Using the tangent double-angle formula in terms of $\tan x$ omits the case $\cos x=0$, so the equations do not have the same solutions.

Use $\tan2\theta=3\tan\theta$ and the tangent double-angle identity.
answer.worked:
The distances from the tower are 150 m at $A$ and 50 m at $B$. Both elevation angles are acute, so $0^\circ<\theta<45^\circ$.

content.prompt:
Consider the trigonometric equation
$$\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ-\theta)\bigr)\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ+\theta)\bigr)=k$$
where $k$ is a constant and $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.

answer.short:
No solution.

The left-hand side simplifies to $2-\dfrac{2}{\cos2\theta}$, which cannot equal 2.
answer.worked:
The original cotangents require $\theta\ne45^\circ,135^\circ,225^\circ,315^\circ$.

Using the sum and difference identities,
$$\begin{align*}\cot(45^\circ-\theta)&=\frac{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta-\sin\theta}\\\cot(45^\circ+\theta)&=\frac{\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}\end{align*}$$

Hence
$$\begin{align*}\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ-\theta)\bigr)\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ+\theta)\bigr)&=\frac{-4\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta}\\\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ-\theta)\bigr)\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ+\theta)\bigr)&=\frac{-2(1-\cos2\theta)}{\cos2\theta}\\\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ-\theta)\bigr)\bigl(1-\cot(45^\circ+\theta)\bigr)&=2-\frac{2}{\cos2\theta}\end{align*}$$

For $k=2$,
$$\begin{align*}2-\frac{2}{\cos2\theta}&=2\\-\frac{2}{\cos2\theta}&=0\end{align*}$$

This is impossible, so there is no solution.

answer.short:
$45^\circ,135^\circ,225^\circ,315^\circ$.

These are limiting values; the original equation is undefined at these angles.
answer.worked:
Using the simplification from part (a),
$$\begin{align*}2-\frac{2}{\cos2\theta}&=k\\\cos2\theta&=\frac{2}{2-k}\end{align*}$$

As $k\to\infty$, $\cos2\theta\to0$ from below. In the given interval, the solutions therefore approach $45^\circ,135^\circ,225^\circ,315^\circ$. The original cotangents are undefined at the limiting angles.

Use $\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$ and consider both signs of the absolute value.
answer.worked:
Since $|\cos2\theta|\ge0$, we need $\cos\theta\ge0$. Let $c=\cos\theta$, so $0\le c\le1$ and $c=|2c^2-1|$.

If $2c^2-1\ge0$,
$$\begin{align*}c&=2c^2-1\\2c^2-c-1&=0\\(2c+1)(c-1)&=0\\c&=1\end{align*}$$

The root $c=-\tfrac12$ is excluded by $c\ge0$.

If $2c^2-1<0$,
$$\begin{align*}c&=1-2c^2\\2c^2+c-1&=0\\(2c-1)(c+1)&=0\\c&=\frac12\end{align*}$$

The root $c=-1$ is excluded by $c\ge0$. The retained roots satisfy their respective sign conditions.

$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta=1:&\quad\theta=0,2\pi\\\cos\theta=\frac12:&\quad\theta=\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3\end{align*}$$

Therefore $\theta=0,\tfrac\pi3,\tfrac{5\pi}3,2\pi$.

children.label: a

answer.short: The base is $2r\cos\theta$ and the height is $r\sin\theta$, so $A=2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta=r^2\sin2\theta$.
answer.worked:
The base is $2r\cos\theta$ and the height is $r\sin\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{rectangle}}&=(2r\cos\theta)(r\sin\theta)\\A_{\text{rectangle}}&=2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\\A_{\text{rectangle}}&=r^2\sin2\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: The area of the rectangle is equal to the area of the kite $OPTP'$. Find the value of $\theta$.

inlines.text: Equate the rectangle area to half the product of the kite’s diagonals.

answer.worked:
The kite has perpendicular diagonals $OT=r$ and $PP'=2r\cos\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{kite}}&=\frac12(r)(2r\cos\theta)\\A_{\text{kite}}&=r^2\cos\theta.\end{align*}$$

Equate the areas and use the sine double-angle identity.

$$\begin{align*}r^2\sin2\theta&=r^2\cos\theta\\2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta&=r^2\cos\theta\\2\sin\theta\cos\theta&=\cos\theta\\2\sin\theta&=1\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\\\theta&=30^\circ.\end{align*}$$

The non-degenerate rectangle has $0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$, so $\cos\theta>0$ and division by $\cos\theta$ is valid.

answer.short:
$\alpha=60^\circ$.

Use $\alpha+2\beta=180^\circ$ and the tangent double-angle identity.
answer.worked:
The base angles are equal, so $\alpha+2\beta=180^\circ$ and $0^\circ<\beta<90^\circ$. Since $\tan\beta>0$ and $\tan\alpha\tan\beta=3$, $\alpha$ is acute; hence $45^\circ<\beta<90^\circ$.

Let $u=\tan\beta>0$.

$$\begin{align*}
\tan\alpha\tan\beta&=3\\
\tan(180^\circ-2\beta)\tan\beta&=3\\
-\tan2\beta\tan\beta&=3\\
-\frac{2u^2}{1-u^2}&=3\\
-2u^2&=3-3u^2\\
u^2&=3\\
u&=\sqrt3\\
\beta&=60^\circ\\
\alpha&=180^\circ-2(60^\circ)\\
\alpha&=60^\circ
\end{align*}$$

spec.sourceRegion: Question 45, between the shared model and part (a)

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
P(t)&=120\bigl((\sin^2t+\cos^2t)^2-2\sin^2t\cos^2t\bigr)\\
P(t)&=120\left(1-\frac12\sin^22t\right)\\
P(t)&=120\left(1-\frac14(1-\cos4t)\right)\\

\end{align*}$$

Thus $A=90$ and $B=30$.

children.prompt: The turbine operates at high efficiency when the power output is at least $105\text{ kW}$. State the values of $t$, in the first five-minute window, for which the power output is at a high efficiency.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
90+30\cos4t&\ge105\\
30\cos4t&\ge15\\
\cos4t&\ge\frac12
\end{align*}$$

The trigonometric arguments are in radians. For each integer $k$,

$$\begin{align*}
-\frac\pi3+2k\pi&\le4t\le\frac\pi3+2k\pi\\
-\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}{2}&\le t\le\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}{2}
\end{align*}$$

Restricting to $0\le t\le5$ gives

$$\begin{aligned}
t\in{}&\left[0,\frac\pi{12}\right]\cup\left[\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac{7\pi}{12}\right]\\
&{}\cup\left[\frac{11\pi}{12},\frac{13\pi}{12}\right]\cup\left[\frac{17\pi}{12},\frac{19\pi}{12}\right]
\end{aligned}$$

where $t$ is in minutes. All endpoints are included because the threshold is “at least” $105\text{ kW}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: For what proportion of the time is the turbine operating at high efficiency?

answer.short:
$\frac13$.

High efficiency occupies one third of each complete period.
answer.worked:
The period of $\cos4t$ is $\frac\pi2$ minutes. In $0\le t\le\frac\pi2$, high efficiency occurs on $\left[0,\frac\pi{12}\right]$ and $\left[\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac\pi2\right]$.

$$\begin{align*}

\text{High-efficiency duration}&=\frac\pi6\text{ minutes}\\
\text{Proportion}&=\frac{\pi/6}{\pi/2}\\
\text{Proportion}&=\frac13
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Show that the trigonometric equation
$$\tan(3x)-\tan(2x)\tan(3x)-\tan(2x)=1$$
has no solutions for any domain of $x$.

answer.short:
No solutions.

The tangent difference identity gives $x=45^\circ+180^\circ k$, but $\tan(2x)$ is undefined at every candidate.
answer.worked:
Rearrange:
$$\begin{align*}\tan(3x)-\tan(2x)&=1+\tan(2x)\tan(3x).\end{align*}$$
The right-hand side cannot be zero: that would require equal tangent values whose product is $-1$, which is impossible for real values.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\tan(3x)-\tan(2x)}{1+\tan(2x)\tan(3x)}&=1\\\tan(3x-2x)&=1\\\tan x&=1\\x&=45^\circ+180^\circ k,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z\\2x&=90^\circ+360^\circ k.\end{align*}$$
At every candidate, $\tan(2x)$ is undefined. Therefore the original equation has no solutions.

answer.short: Each sine is at most 1, so their sum can equal 2 only when both equal 1.
answer.worked: Since $\sin(2x)\le1$ and $\sin(3x)\le1$, if either were less than 1 their sum would be less than 2. Therefore both equal 1 simultaneously.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Show that the solution of $\sin(2x)=1$, across any domain of $x$, can be expressed as

$$\frac{\pi}{4}+m\pi,$$

where $m$ is an integer.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2x&=\frac{\pi}{2}+2m\pi\\x&=\frac{\pi}{4}+m\pi\end{align*}$$

Here $m\in\mathbb Z$, because sine equals 1 at $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and repeats every $2\pi$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that similarly, any solution of $\sin(3x)=1$ must be in the form $x=\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2n\pi}{3}$, where $n$ is an integer.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}3x&=\frac{\pi}{2}+2n\pi\\x&=\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2n\pi}{3}\end{align*}$$

Here $n\in\mathbb Z$, using the same $2\pi$ period.

answer.short:
No solutions.

Equating the general solutions gives $12m-8n=-1$, impossible because the left side is even.
answer.worked:
Suppose a solution exists. The two sine terms sum to 2, so by part (a), both must equal 1. Therefore the expressions from parts (b) and (c) must agree for integers $m,n$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{\pi}{4}+m\pi&=\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2n\pi}{3}\\3+12m&=2+8n\\12m-8n&=-1\end{align*}$$

The left side is even, whereas $-1$ is odd. This contradiction proves that there are no solutions.

content.prompt: Let $\cos\alpha+\cos\beta=a$ and $\sec\alpha+\sec\beta=b$, where $b\ne0$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}b&=\frac{1}{\cos\alpha}+\frac{1}{\cos\beta}\\b&=\frac{\cos\alpha+\cos\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}\\b&=\frac{a}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}\\\cos\alpha\cos\beta&=\frac{a}{b}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, show that $\cos\alpha$ and $\cos\beta$ are solutions of $bx^2-abx+a=0$.

answer.short:
$bx^2-abx+a=0$ has roots $\cos\alpha$ and $\cos\beta$.

Use their sum $a$ and product $a/b$.
answer.worked:
The quadratic with roots $\cos\alpha$ and $\cos\beta$ is

$$\begin{align*}(x-\cos\alpha)(x-\cos\beta)&=0\\x^2-(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta)x+\cos\alpha\cos\beta&=0\\x^2-ax+\frac{a}{b}&=0\\bx^2-abx+a&=0\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
One angle is $60^\circ$ or $300^\circ$; the other is $\cos^{-1}(\frac14)$ or $360^\circ-\cos^{-1}(\frac14)$, in either order.

The cosine values are $\frac12$ and $\frac14$, found from the quadratic.
answer.worked:
Substitute $a=\frac34$ and $b=6$ into part (b).

$$\begin{align*}6x^2-\frac92x+\frac34&=0\\8x^2-6x+1&=0\\(2x-1)(4x-1)&=0\\x&=\frac12\text{ or }\frac14\end{align*}$$

Since the two cosine values sum to $\frac34$, one is $\frac12$ and the other is $\frac14$.

$$\begin{align*}\cos\alpha&=\frac12\\\alpha&=60^\circ\text{ or }300^\circ\\\cos\beta&=\frac14\\\beta&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right)\text{ or }360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right)\end{align*}$$

The roles of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ may be interchanged. Every such pair satisfies the original equations: the cosine sum is $\frac12+\frac14=\frac34$, and the secant sum is $2+4=6$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\cos40^\circ\cos20^\circ-2\sin40^\circ\sin20^\circ&=2\cos(40^\circ+20^\circ)\\2\cos40^\circ\cos20^\circ-2\sin40^\circ\sin20^\circ&=2\cos60^\circ\\2\cos40^\circ\cos20^\circ-2\sin40^\circ\sin20^\circ&=1\end{align*}$$
Thus $\theta=20^\circ$ satisfies the equation.

children.prompt:
Show that any solution $\alpha$ of the equation satisfies
$$8x^3-6x-1=0,$$
where $x=\cos\alpha$.

answer.short:
$8x^3-6x-1=0$, where $x=\cos\alpha$.

Use the cosine sum identity, expand the double-angle terms and substitute $x=\cos\alpha$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\cos3\alpha&=\cos2\alpha\cos\alpha-\sin2\alpha\sin\alpha\\\cos3\alpha&=(2\cos^2\alpha-1)\cos\alpha-2\sin^2\alpha\cos\alpha\\\cos3\alpha&=2\cos^3\alpha-\cos\alpha-2(1-\cos^2\alpha)\cos\alpha\\\cos3\alpha&=4\cos^3\alpha-3\cos\alpha\end{align*}$$
The given equation therefore gives
$$\begin{align*}2\cos3\alpha&=1\\8\cos^3\alpha-6\cos\alpha&=1\\8\cos^3\alpha-6\cos\alpha-1&=0\end{align*}$$
Substituting $x=\cos\alpha$ gives $8x^3-6x-1=0$.

answer.short:
$\cos20^\circ$ is irrational.

The only possible rational roots of $8x^3-6x-1=0$ are $\pm1,\pm\frac12,\pm\frac14,\pm\frac18$; none satisfies the equation.
answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=8x^3-6x-1$. By the rational root theorem, the only possible rational roots are $\pm1,\pm\frac12,\pm\frac14,\pm\frac18$.
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=1, &P(-1)&=-3\\P\left(\frac12\right)&=-3, &P\left(-\frac12\right)&=1\\P\left(\frac14\right)&=-\frac{19}{8}, &P\left(-\frac14\right)&=\frac38\\P\left(\frac18\right)&=-\frac{111}{64}, &P\left(-\frac18\right)&=-\frac{17}{64}\end{align*}$$
None is zero, so $P(x)=0$ has no rational roots. By parts (a) and (b), $\cos20^\circ$ is a root of $P(x)=0$. Hence $\cos20^\circ$ is irrational.

content.prompt: Explain why a substitution like $x=\sin\theta$ to reduce a polynomial to $\sin3\theta=\frac12$ needs extra care, whereas $x=\cos\theta$ to reduce to $\cos3\theta=\frac12$ does not? What is it about the first substitution that makes it so much more tricky?

answer.short:
For increasing $\theta\ge0$, sine starts repeating values after $\theta=\frac\pi2$, while cosine is one-to-one on $[0,\pi]$. Sine may repeat values before all three distinct polynomial roots have been found.

Continue finding angles and discard repeated values of $x$.
answer.worked:
For increasing $\theta\ge0$, $\sin\theta$ starts repeating values after $\theta=\frac\pi2$, whereas $\cos\theta$ is one-to-one on $[0,\pi]$.

For $\sin3\theta=\frac12$, the first positive angles are
$$\theta=\frac\pi{18},\frac{5\pi}{18},\frac{13\pi}{18},\frac{17\pi}{18},\frac{25\pi}{18},\ldots$$
But $\sin\frac{13\pi}{18}=\sin\frac{5\pi}{18}$ and $\sin\frac{17\pi}{18}=\sin\frac\pi{18}$. Thus the first three angles give only two distinct values of $x$; continuing to $\frac{25\pi}{18}$ gives the third.

For $\cos3\theta=\frac12$, the first three nonnegative angles are $\frac\pi9$, $\frac{5\pi}9$ and $\frac{7\pi}9$. All lie in $[0,\pi]$, so their cosine values are distinct.

inlines.text: Bob and Mary are tasked with solving
They both think the other’s method is incorrect. Who is correct, and why?

answer.short:
Both methods are correct: Bob obtains $\cos3\theta=\frac12$, while Mary obtains $\sin3\theta=-\frac12$.

Both identities reduce the cubic to a trigonometric equation; retain three distinct values of $x$.
answer.worked:
Both methods are correct.

With Bob’s substitution $x=\cos\theta$,
$$\begin{align*}
8\cos^3\theta-6\cos\theta-1&=0\\
2\cos3\theta-1&=0\\
\cos3\theta&=\frac12.
\end{align*}$$
With Mary’s substitution $x=\sin\theta$,
$$\begin{align*}
8\sin^3\theta-6\sin\theta-1&=0\\
-2\sin3\theta-1&=0\\
\sin3\theta&=-\frac12.
\end{align*}$$
Both follow from the supplied identities and give the same three distinct polynomial roots. Mary must take care to discard repeated sine values and continue until all three roots have been found.

answer.worked:
Using $\cos3x=4\cos^3x-3\cos x$,
$$\begin{align*}\cos3x+1&=0\\\cos3x&=-1.\end{align*}$$
Since $0\le3x\le6\pi$,
$$\begin{align*}3x&=\pi,3\pi,5\pi\\x&=\frac\pi3,\pi,\frac{5\pi}3.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let $t=\tan x$ and $P(t)=t^3-2t^2-5t+6$. Since $P(1)=0$,
$$\begin{align*}P(t)&=(t-1)(t^2-t-6)\\P(t)&=(t-1)(t-3)(t+2).\end{align*}$$
Thus $\tan x=1,3,-2$. For $0\le x\le2\pi$,
$$\begin{align*}\tan x=1:\quad x&=\frac\pi4,\frac{5\pi}4\\\tan x=3:\quad x&=\tan^{-1}3,\pi+\tan^{-1}3\\\tan x=-2:\quad x&=\pi-\tan^{-1}2,2\pi-\tan^{-1}2.\end{align*}$$
Hence $x=\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{5\pi}4,1.25,4.39,2.03,5.18$, with non-exact values rounded to two decimal places.

answer.worked:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\cos4\theta&=2\cos^2(2\theta)-1\\\cos4\theta&=2(2\cos^2\theta-1)^2-1\\\cos4\theta&=2(4\cos^4\theta-4\cos^2\theta+1)-1\\\cos4\theta&=8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\pm\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right),\ \pm\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}8\right)$.

Substitute $x=\cos\theta$ and use part (a) to obtain $\cos4\theta=0$.
answer.worked:
Let $x=\cos\theta$, taking $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$ so that distinct angles give distinct cosine values. By part (a),
$$\begin{align*}8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1&=0\\\cos4\theta&=0\\4\theta&=\frac\pi2,\ \frac{3\pi}2,\ \frac{5\pi}2,\ \frac{7\pi}2\\\theta&=\frac\pi8,\ \frac{3\pi}8,\ \frac{5\pi}8,\ \frac{7\pi}8.\end{align*}$$
Hence $x=\pm\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right),\ \pm\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}8\right)$. These four distinct roots account for all roots of the quartic.

children.prompt: Find the exact values of $\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right)$ and $\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}8\right)$.

answer.short:
$\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right)=\frac12\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}$,

$\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}8\right)=-\frac12\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}$.

Solve the quartic as a quadratic in $x^2$ and select the values and signs from the angles.
answer.worked:
Put $u=x^2$ in the quartic from part (b).
$$\begin{align*}8u^2-8u+1&=0\\u&=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{64-32}}{16}\\u&=\frac{2\pm\sqrt2}{4}.\end{align*}$$
The larger squared value belongs to $\cos(\pi/8)$, which is positive. Since $\cos(5\pi/8)=-\cos(3\pi/8)$, its squared value is the smaller one and its sign is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right)&=\sqrt{\frac{2+\sqrt2}{4}}\\\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right)&=\frac12\sqrt{2+\sqrt2},\\\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}8\right)&=-\sqrt{\frac{2-\sqrt2}{4}}\\\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}8\right)&=-\frac12\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=\sqrt2\sin\left(\frac\pi4\right),\ \sqrt2\sin\left(\frac\pi{12}\right),\ \sqrt2\sin\left(-\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)$.

Equivalently, $x=1,\ \frac{\sqrt3-1}{2},\ -\frac{\sqrt3+1}{2}$.

The substitution gives $\sin3\theta=1/\sqrt2$; retain three distinct values of $x$.
answer.worked:
Let $x=\sqrt2\sin\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}4\sqrt2\sin^3\theta-3\sqrt2\sin\theta+1&=0\\4\sin^3\theta-3\sin\theta&=-\frac1{\sqrt2}\\\sin3\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\\3\theta&=\frac\pi4,\ \frac{3\pi}4,\ \frac{9\pi}4,\ \frac{11\pi}4,\ \frac{17\pi}4,\ldots\\\theta&=\frac\pi{12},\ \frac\pi4,\ \frac{3\pi}4,\ \frac{11\pi}{12},\ \frac{17\pi}{12},\ldots\end{align*}$$
The angles $3\pi/4$ and $11\pi/12$ repeat the sine values from $\pi/4$ and $\pi/12$. The next distinct value is $\sin(17\pi/12)=-\sin(5\pi/12)$.

Thus the three distinct roots are
$$x=\sqrt2\sin\left(\frac\pi4\right),\quad\sqrt2\sin\left(\frac\pi{12}\right),\quad\sqrt2\sin\left(-\frac{5\pi}{12}\right).$$
Using the difference and sum identities at $\pi/4$ and $\pi/6$, these are
$$x=1,\quad\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2},\quad-\frac{\sqrt3+1}{2}.$$
Three distinct roots account for all roots of the cubic.

Let $x=\sec\theta$, where $\cos\theta\ne0$.

Hence
$$x=\sec\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right),\quad\sec\left(\frac{4\pi}{9}\right),\quad\sec\left(\frac{8\pi}{9}\right).$$

content.prompt: Solve the following. You may assume the identity $\tan4\theta=\dfrac{4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta}{1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta}$.

answer.short:
$x=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right),\ \tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{16}\right),\ \tan\left(\frac{9\pi}{16}\right),\ \tan\left(\frac{13\pi}{16}\right)$.

Rearrange the substituted quartic to obtain $\tan4\theta=1$.
answer.worked:
Let $x=\tan\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan^4\theta+4\tan^3\theta-6\tan^2\theta-4\tan\theta+1&=0\\1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta&=4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta.\end{align*}$$
The denominator of the supplied identity is nonzero at a root: otherwise its numerator would also be zero, requiring $\tan\theta=0,1$ or $-1$, none of which makes the denominator zero. Thus
$$\begin{align*}\tan4\theta&=1\\4\theta&=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi\\\theta&=\frac{\pi}{16}+\frac{k\pi}{4},\quad k\in\mathbb Z.\end{align*}$$
For $k=0,1,2,3$, the four distinct roots are
$$x=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right),\quad\tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{16}\right),\quad\tan\left(\frac{9\pi}{16}\right),\quad\tan\left(\frac{13\pi}{16}\right).$$
These exhaust the roots of the quartic.

answer.short:

Rewrite the substituted equation in $\tan\theta$ to obtain $\tan4\theta=1$.
answer.worked:
Let $x=2\cot\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}16\cot^4\theta-64\cot^3\theta-96\cot^2\theta+64\cot\theta+16&=0\\\cot^4\theta-4\cot^3\theta-6\cot^2\theta+4\cot\theta+1&=0.\end{align*}$$
Since $x=0$ is not a root, $\cot\theta\ne0$. Multiply by $\tan^4\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}1-4\tan\theta-6\tan^2\theta+4\tan^3\theta+\tan^4\theta&=0\\1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta&=4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta.\end{align*}$$
The denominator of the supplied identity cannot vanish here: simultaneous zero numerator would require $\tan\theta=0,1$ or $-1$, whose denominator values are $1,-4,-4$. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}\tan4\theta&=1\\4\theta&=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi\\\theta&=\frac{\pi}{16}+\frac{k\pi}{4},\quad k\in\mathbb Z.\end{align*}$$
For $k=0,1,2,3$,
$$x=2\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right),\quad2\cot\left(\frac{5\pi}{16}\right),\quad2\cot\left(\frac{9\pi}{16}\right),\quad2\cot\left(\frac{13\pi}{16}\right).$$
These four values are defined and distinct, so they exhaust the roots of the quartic.

children.prompt: Use the identity $\tan4\theta=\dfrac{4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta}{1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta}$ to find the values of $\theta$ such that $x=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\tan\theta$ is a solution of $P(x)=0$.

answer.short:
$\theta=\dfrac\pi{12}+\dfrac{k\pi}{4}$, $k\in\mathbb Z$.

Four representatives modulo $\pi$ are $\dfrac\pi{12},\dfrac\pi3,\dfrac{7\pi}{12},\dfrac{5\pi}6$. The substitution reduces the equation to $\tan4\theta=\sqrt3$.
answer.worked:
Let $t=\tan\theta$, so $x=t/\sqrt3$.
$$\begin{align*}P(t/\sqrt3)&=t^4+\frac4{\sqrt3}t^3-6t^2-\frac4{\sqrt3}t+1\\P(t/\sqrt3)&=(1-6t^2+t^4)-\frac1{\sqrt3}(4t-4t^3).\end{align*}$$
Thus $P(x)=0$ gives
$$\begin{align*}1-6t^2+t^4&=\frac1{\sqrt3}(4t-4t^3)\\\frac{4t-4t^3}{1-6t^2+t^4}&=\sqrt3\\\tan4\theta&=\sqrt3\\4\theta&=\frac\pi3+k\pi\\\theta&=\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}{4},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.\end{align*}$$
The denominator cannot be zero at a solution: a zero denominator would require $4t-4t^3=0$, but $t=0,\pm1$ do not make the denominator zero. Four representatives modulo $\pi$ are $\pi/12,\pi/3,7\pi/12,5\pi/6$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why $(x-1)(3x+1)$ is a factor of $P(x)$.

answer.short: $\theta=\pi/3$ and $5\pi/6$ give $x=1$ and $-1/3$. By the factor theorem, $(x-1)(3x+1)$ is a factor.
answer.worked:
$\theta=\pi/3$ and $5\pi/6$ are solutions from part (a).
$$\begin{align*}\frac1{\sqrt3}\tan\frac\pi3&=1\\\frac1{\sqrt3}\tan\frac{5\pi}6&=-\frac13.\end{align*}$$
Hence $P(1)=P(-1/3)=0$. By the factor theorem, $x-1$ and $x+1/3$ are distinct factors, so their product, equivalently $(x-1)(3x+1)$, is a factor of $P(x)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: By finding the other zeroes of $P(x)$ in surd form, find the exact value of $\tan\left(\dfrac\pi{12}\right)$, giving reasons.

answer.short:
Other zeroes: $-1\pm\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{3}$.

$\tan(\pi/12)=2-\sqrt3$. Divide out the known factors, then select the positive tangent value.
answer.worked:
Dividing out the factors from part (b),
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x-1)(3x+1)(3x^2+6x-1)\\3x^2+6x-1&=0\\x&=\frac{-6\pm\sqrt{36+12}}6\\x&=-1\pm\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}.\end{align*}$$
The other tangent values are therefore
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\sqrt3x\\\tan\theta&=-\sqrt3\pm2.\end{align*}$$
The known roots $1$ and $-1/3$ correspond to $\theta=\pi/3$ and $5\pi/6$ modulo $\pi$. Thus $\pi/12$ corresponds to one of the other roots. Since $0<\pi/12<\pi/2$, its tangent is positive:
$$\tan\frac\pi{12}=2-\sqrt3.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, find the exact value of $\cos\left(\dfrac\pi{24}\right)$.

answer.short:
$\cos(\pi/24)=\dfrac12\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}$.

Solve the quartic as a quadratic in $x^2$ and choose the larger positive root.
answer.worked:
Let $y=x^2$ in the equation from part (a).

Use $x=2\sin\theta$ and retain three distinct sine values.
answer.worked:
Let $x=2\sin\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}8\sin^3\theta-6\sin\theta+1&=0\\3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta&=\frac12\\\sin3\theta&=\frac12.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}3\theta&=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}6,\frac{13\pi}6,\frac{17\pi}6,\frac{25\pi}6\\\theta&=\frac\pi{18},\frac{5\pi}{18},\frac{13\pi}{18},\frac{17\pi}{18},\frac{25\pi}{18}.\end{align*}$$
The third and fourth sine values repeat the second and first. The fifth supplies the negative root:
$$\sin\frac{25\pi}{18}=-\sin\frac{7\pi}{18}.$$
Hence the three distinct roots are
$$x=2\sin\frac\pi{18},\quad2\sin\frac{5\pi}{18},\quad-2\sin\frac{7\pi}{18}.$$

answer.short:
$\dfrac32$.

Use the sum and pairwise products of the cubic roots to obtain their sum of squares.
answer.worked:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots from part (a). For $x^3-3x+1=0$,
$$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0,\qquad\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma=-3.$$
Thus
$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)\\\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=0-2(-3)\\\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=6.\end{align*}$$
Each root is twice its corresponding sine, with a sign that disappears on squaring. Therefore the required sum is $6/4=3/2$.

$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)\\\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=\frac23.\end{align*}$$

To match $4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$, compare coefficient ratios:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{r^3}{6r}&=\frac43\\r^2&=8\\r&=2\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
Then
$$\begin{align*}P(2\sqrt2\cos\theta)&=16\sqrt2\cos^3\theta-12\sqrt2\cos\theta+4\\P(2\sqrt2\cos\theta)&=4\sqrt2\cos3\theta+4.\end{align*}$$
Thus $P(x)=0$ becomes $\cos3\theta=-1/\sqrt2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, find the zeroes of $P(x)$ using two different methods to find the exact value of $\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)$.

Zeroes: $2,\ -1+\sqrt3,\ -1-\sqrt3$.

$\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4}$.

Compare the factorised roots with the scaled cosine roots, then use $\cos(\pi-u)=-\cos u$.

Algebraically, $P(2)=0$, so
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x-2)(x^2+2x-2)\\x^2+2x-2&=0\\x&=-1\pm\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
The zeroes are $2,-1+\sqrt3,-1-\sqrt3$.

Using part (a), $\cos3\theta=-1/\sqrt2$. For $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$,
$$3\theta=\frac{3\pi}{4},\ \frac{5\pi}{4},\ \frac{11\pi}{4},\qquad\theta=\frac\pi4,\ \frac{5\pi}{12},\ \frac{11\pi}{12}.$$
Hence the same zeroes are
$$2\sqrt2\cos\left(\frac\pi4\right),\quad2\sqrt2\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right),\quad2\sqrt2\cos\left(\frac{11\pi}{12}\right).$$
The second value is positive and less than $2$, so
$$\begin{align*}2\sqrt2\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)&=-1+\sqrt3\\\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)&=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\\\cos\left(\frac{7\pi}{12}\right)&=-\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)\\\cos\left(\frac{7\pi}{12}\right)&=\frac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Solve $\cos3\theta=\cos\theta-\sqrt2$ for $0\leq\theta\leq2\pi$. Give exact angles where possible; otherwise give answers in radians correct to two decimal places.

Hint: Use the identity for $\cos3\theta$.

answer.short:
$\theta=\dfrac\pi4,\ \dfrac{7\pi}4,\ 1.12,\ 5.16$ radians, with decimal values correct to two decimal places.

Expand $\cos3\theta$, factor the cubic in $\cos\theta$ and reject the root below $-1$.
answer.worked:
Let $u=\cos\theta$ and use $\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}4u^3-3u&=u-\sqrt2\\4u^3-4u+\sqrt2&=0\\\left(u-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)(4u^2+2\sqrt2u-2)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus
$$u=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\qquad u=\frac{-\sqrt2+\sqrt{10}}4,\qquad u=\frac{-\sqrt2-\sqrt{10}}4.$$
The last value is below $-1$, so it cannot equal $\cos\theta$.

For $u=\sqrt2/2$, the angles are $\theta=\pi/4,7\pi/4$. For the other valid root, let
$$\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{10}-\sqrt2}{4}\right).$$
The angles are $\theta=\alpha,2\pi-\alpha$, giving $1.12,5.16$ radians to two decimal places.

Therefore $\theta=\pi/4,7\pi/4,1.12,5.16$ radians.

children.label: b

$\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4}$.

Expand the identities, divide by the nonzero cosine and take the positive root of $4s^2+2s-1=0$.
answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$ and $s=\sin\theta$. By part (a),
$$4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta.$$

$$\begin{align*}4\cos^2\theta-3&=2s\\4(1-s^2)-3&=2s\\4s^2+2s-1&=0\\s&=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+16}}{8}\\s&=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{4}.\end{align*}$$

$$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{10}\right)=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Let $x=\tan^2\theta$. By using identities for $\tan2\theta$ and $\tan3\theta$, show that if $\tan2\theta\tan3\theta=1$, then
$$5x^2-10x+1=0.$$

answer.short:
$5x^2-10x+1=0$.

Expand the tangent identities and substitute $x=\tan^2\theta$.
answer.worked:
Let $t=\tan\theta$, so $x=t^2$. Using the tangent identities,
$$\begin{align*}\tan2\theta\tan3\theta&=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}\cdot\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}\\\tan2\theta\tan3\theta&=\frac{6t^2-2t^4}{1-4t^2+3t^4}.\end{align*}$$
The given product is defined and equals $1$, so
$$\begin{align*}6t^2-2t^4&=1-4t^2+3t^4\\5t^4-10t^2+1&=0\\5x^2-10x+1&=0.\end{align*}$$

$$\tan^2(18^\circ)=\frac{5-2\sqrt5}{5}.$$

$$\begin{align*}\cos36^\circ&=\frac{1-\tan^2(18^\circ)}{1+\tan^2(18^\circ)}\\\cos36^\circ&=\frac{1-\frac{5-2\sqrt5}{5}}{1+\frac{5-2\sqrt5}{5}}\\\cos36^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt5}{5-\sqrt5}\\\cos36^\circ&=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Given $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $\tan\alpha$, $\tan\beta$ and $\tan\gamma$ are roots of the equation $x^3-kx^2+kx-1=0$, find the value of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$.

answer.short:
$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Use the cubic’s root sums and product in the three-angle tangent identity, then select the angle using its quadrant and range.
answer.worked:
Let $a=\tan\alpha$, $b=\tan\beta$, $c=\tan\gamma$ and $S=\alpha+\beta+\gamma$. The root–coefficient relationships give
$$a+b+c=k,\qquad ab+bc+ca=k,\qquad abc=1.$$
The roots are nonnegative and have product $1$, so they are positive. Their sum satisfies $k\ge3$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan S&=\frac{a+b+c-abc}{1-ab-bc-ca}\\\tan S&=\frac{k-1}{1-k}\\\tan S&=-1.\end{align*}$$
To determine the quadrant, expand the three-angle sine and cosine:
$$\begin{align*}\sin S&=\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma\,(k-1)>0\\\cos S&=\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma\,(1-k)<0.\end{align*}$$
Since $0<S<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, these signs place $S$ in the second quadrant. Therefore
$$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac{3\pi}{4}.$$

$r=2\sqrt{\frac p3}$, so $x=2\sqrt{\frac p3}\cos\theta$ and $\cos3\theta=-\frac{3q}{2p}\sqrt{\frac3p}$.

Choose $r^2=\frac{4p}{3}$ to match the supplied triple-angle identity.
answer.worked:
Substitute $x=r\cos\theta$, choosing $r>0$ with $r^2=\frac{4p}{3}$.
$$\begin{align*}P(r\cos\theta)&=r^3\cos^3\theta-pr\cos\theta+q\\P(r\cos\theta)&=\frac{pr}{3}(4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta)+q\\P(r\cos\theta)&=\frac{pr}{3}\cos3\theta+q.\end{align*}$$
Since $pr>0$, $P(x)=0$ is equivalent to
$$\begin{align*}\cos3\theta&=-\frac{3q}{pr}\\\cos3\theta&=-\frac{3q}{2p}\sqrt{\frac3p}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, show that if $P(x)$ has three real zeroes, counting multiplicity, then $4p^3-27q^2\ge0$.

answer.short:
$4p^3-27q^2\ge0$.

Three real roots allow the substitution in part (a); apply $|\cos3\theta|\le1$ and square.
answer.worked:
Let the three real roots be $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. The root relationships give $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ and $\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma=-p$. Thus
$$\begin{align*}(\beta-\gamma)^2&=(\beta+\gamma)^2-4\beta\gamma\\(\beta-\gamma)^2&=\alpha^2-4(\alpha^2-p)\\(\beta-\gamma)^2&=4p-3\alpha^2\ge0.\end{align*}$$
Hence $|\alpha|\le2\sqrt{p/3}$, so write $\alpha=2\sqrt{p/3}\cos\theta$ for a real $\theta$. Part (a) and the range of cosine give
$$\begin{align*}\left|\frac{3q}{2p}\sqrt{\frac3p}\right|&\le1\\\frac{27q^2}{4p^3}&\le1\\4p^3-27q^2&\ge0.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Solve $3\cos x-\sqrt3\sin x=2\sqrt3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.

answer.worked:
Write $3\cos x-\sqrt3\sin x=R\cos(x+\alpha)$, where $R>0$.
$$\begin{align*}R&=\sqrt{3^2+(\sqrt3)^2}\\R&=2\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
Matching coefficients gives
$$\cos\alpha=\frac3{2\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}2,\qquad\sin\alpha=\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sqrt3}=\frac12,$$
so $\alpha=\frac\pi6$.
$$\begin{align*}2\sqrt3\cos\left(x+\frac\pi6\right)&=2\sqrt3\\\cos\left(x+\frac\pi6\right)&=1.\end{align*}$$
For $0\le x\le2\pi$, the angle $x+\frac\pi6$ lies in $[\frac\pi6,\frac{13\pi}6]$. The only angle in this interval with cosine $1$ is $2\pi$.
$$\begin{align*}x+\frac\pi6&=2\pi\\x&=\frac{11\pi}6.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Use the identity $\cos4\theta=8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1$ and $x=\cos\theta$ to find the zeroes of $P(x)$ in trigonometric form.

answer.worked:
For $x=\cos\theta$, the supplied identity gives
$$\begin{align*}P(\cos\theta)&=8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1\\P(\cos\theta)&=\cos4\theta.\end{align*}$$

Choose $0\le\theta\le\pi$ to obtain distinct cosine values. Then
$$\begin{align*}\cos4\theta&=0\\4\theta&=\frac\pi2,\ \frac{3\pi}2,\ \frac{5\pi}2,\ \frac{7\pi}2\\\theta&=\frac\pi8,\ \frac{3\pi}8,\ \frac{5\pi}8,\ \frac{7\pi}8.\end{align*}$$

These give four distinct zeroes, so they account for all zeroes of the quartic:
$$x=\pm\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right),\ \pm\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}8\right).$$

answer.short:
$\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}}2$.

Solve the quadratic in $x^2$ and select the larger positive root, since $\cos(\pi/8)>\cos(3\pi/8)$.
answer.worked:
Put $u=x^2$. Using the quadratic formula,
$$\begin{align*}8u^2-8u+1&=0\\u&=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{(-8)^2-4(8)(1)}}{16}\\u&=\frac{8\pm4\sqrt2}{16}\\u&=\frac{2\pm\sqrt2}{4}.\end{align*}$$

Thus the four zeroes are
$$x=\pm\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}}2,\quad\pm\frac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}}2.$$

From part (a), the positive zeroes are $\cos(\pi/8)$ and $\cos(3\pi/8)$. Since cosine decreases on $[0,\pi]$, $\cos(\pi/8)>\cos(3\pi/8)$. Therefore the larger positive root is
$$\cos\left(\frac\pi8\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}}2.$$

content.prompt: Prove the following identities.

answer.short: Expand $\sin(\alpha+\beta)$ and divide each term by $\sin\alpha\sin\beta$ to obtain $\cot\alpha+\cot\beta$.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}{\sin\alpha\sin\beta}&=\frac{\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta}{\sin\alpha\sin\beta}\\\frac{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}{\sin\alpha\sin\beta}&=\frac{\cos\beta}{\sin\beta}+\frac{\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}\\\frac{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}{\sin\alpha\sin\beta}&=\cot\alpha+\cot\beta.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Prove identities by expanding a compound angle.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The sine sum expansion separates into the two requested cotangent terms.

answer.short:
The left-hand side equals $\tan(\alpha+\beta)$.

Expand the compound angles, factor $\cos\alpha$ from both numerator and denominator, then cancel.
answer.worked:
Let $N$ and $D$ be the numerator and denominator of the left-hand side. Expand each compound angle:
$$\begin{align*}N&=\sin\beta+\sin\alpha(\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta)\\N&=(1-\sin^2\alpha)\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\cos\beta\\N&=\cos\alpha(\cos\alpha\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\cos\beta)\\N&=\cos\alpha\sin(\alpha+\beta).\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}D&=\cos\beta-\sin\alpha(\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta)\\D&=(1-\sin^2\alpha)\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\sin\beta\\D&=\cos\alpha(\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta)\\D&=\cos\alpha\cos(\alpha+\beta).\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\cos(\alpha+\beta)}{\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin(\alpha+\beta)}&=\frac{\cos\alpha\sin(\alpha+\beta)}{\cos\alpha\cos(\alpha+\beta)}\\\frac{\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\cos(\alpha+\beta)}{\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin(\alpha+\beta)}&=\tan(\alpha+\beta).\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Show that $\dfrac{\sin\alpha+\sin(45^\circ-\alpha)}{\cos\alpha+\cos(45^\circ-\alpha)}=\tan 22.5^\circ$.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt2}=\tan 22.5^\circ$.

Expand the differences and factor the numerator; use the double-angle formulas to identify the constant.
answer.worked:
Using $\sin45^\circ=\cos45^\circ=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$,

$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\alpha+\sin(45^\circ-\alpha)}{\cos\alpha+\cos(45^\circ-\alpha)}&=\frac{\sin\alpha+\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha)}{\cos\alpha+\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\cos\alpha+\sin\alpha)}\\\frac{\sin\alpha+\sin(45^\circ-\alpha)}{\cos\alpha+\cos(45^\circ-\alpha)}&=\frac{(\sqrt2-1)\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha+(\sqrt2+1)\cos\alpha}\\\frac{\sin\alpha+\sin(45^\circ-\alpha)}{\cos\alpha+\cos(45^\circ-\alpha)}&=\frac{(\sqrt2-1)[\sin\alpha+(\sqrt2+1)\cos\alpha]}{\sin\alpha+(\sqrt2+1)\cos\alpha}\\\frac{\sin\alpha+\sin(45^\circ-\alpha)}{\cos\alpha+\cos(45^\circ-\alpha)}&=\sqrt2-1.\end{align*}$$

Set $\theta=22.5^\circ$, so $2\theta=45^\circ$. The double-angle formulas give

$$\begin{align*}\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{2\sin22.5^\circ\cos22.5^\circ}{2\cos^2 22.5^\circ}\\\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{\sin45^\circ}{1+\cos45^\circ}\\\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt2/2}{1+\sqrt2/2}\\\tan22.5^\circ&=\frac1{1+\sqrt2}=\sqrt2-1.\end{align*}$$

Hence the identity holds wherever the original quotient is defined.

answer.short:
$\dfrac18\sin8\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\cos\theta\cos2\theta\cos4\theta$.

content.prompt: Solve the following equations in the domain $0\le x\le2\pi$ by first converting to auxiliary angle form.

answer.worked:
Write the left-hand side as $R\sin(x-\alpha)$.

$$\begin{align*}R\cos\alpha&=1\\R\sin\alpha&=\sqrt3\\R&=\sqrt{1+3}=2\\\alpha&=\frac\pi3.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x&=2\sin\left(x-\frac\pi3\right)\\2\sin\left(x-\frac\pi3\right)&=0\\x-\frac\pi3&=0,\pi\\x&=\frac\pi3,\frac{4\pi}3.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Equate coefficients in an auxiliary sine form, then solve the transformed equation.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Pages 60–61 prescribe coefficient matching, positive amplitude and solving through auxiliary-angle form; the shared source instruction explicitly requires this method.

answer.worked:
Write the left-hand side as $R\sin(x+\alpha)$.

$$\begin{align*}R\sin\alpha&=\sqrt3\\R\cos\alpha&=3\\R&=\sqrt{3+9}=2\sqrt3\\\alpha&=\frac\pi6.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\sqrt3\cos x+3\sin x&=2\sqrt3\sin\left(x+\frac\pi6\right)\\2\sqrt3\sin\left(x+\frac\pi6\right)&=3\\\sin\left(x+\frac\pi6\right)&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\x+\frac\pi6&=\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3\\x&=\frac\pi6,\frac\pi2.\end{align*}$$

These are all solutions for $0\le x\le2\pi$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that $\tan\left(\dfrac\pi{12}\right)$ is a root of the equation

$$t^3-3t^2-3t+1=0$$

by considering the expansion of $\tan(3\theta)$.

answer.worked:
Let $t=\tan\theta$. Using the sum and double-angle formulas,

$$\begin{align*}\tan3\theta&=\frac{\tan2\theta+\tan\theta}{1-\tan2\theta\tan\theta}\\\tan3\theta&=\frac{\frac{2t}{1-t^2}+t}{1-\frac{2t^2}{1-t^2}}\\\tan3\theta&=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}.\end{align*}$$

Set $\theta=\pi/12$, so $\tan3\theta=\tan(\pi/4)=1$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}&=1\\3t-t^3&=1-3t^2\\t^3-3t^2-3t+1&=0.\end{align*}$$

Thus $\tan(\pi/12)$ is a root.

teachingContext.methodNote: Expand tan(2θ+θ), substitute the tangent double-angle formula and set θ=π/12.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Page 60 supplies both needed identities; page 61 explains connecting trigonometric and polynomial equations. The question explicitly requests the tan(3θ) expansion.

answer.short:
$\tan\left(\dfrac\pi{12}\right)=2-\sqrt3$.

Factor the cubic as $(t+1)(t^2-4t+1)$ and select the root in $(0,1)$.
answer.worked:
Let $P(t)=t^3-3t^2-3t+1$.

$$\begin{align*}P(-1)&=-1-3+3+1\\P(-1)&=0\\P(t)&=(t+1)(t^2-4t+1).\end{align*}$$

By part (a), $t=\tan(\pi/12)$ is a root. Since $0<\tan(\pi/12)<1$, the root $-1$ is excluded.

$$\begin{align*}t^2-4t+1&=0\\t&=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{16-4}}2\\t&=2\pm\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$

Only $2-\sqrt3$ lies in $(0,1)$, so $\tan(\pi/12)=2-\sqrt3$.

teachingContext.mappingNote: Page 61 explicitly prescribes the factor theorem for trigonometric polynomial equations; the answer evidence supplies this factorisation and range selection.

answer.worked:
The remaining root is $2+\sqrt3$. Since $5\pi/12=\pi/2-\pi/12$,

$$\begin{align*}\tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)&=\frac1{\tan(\pi/12)}\\\tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)&=\frac1{2-\sqrt3}\\\tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)&=\frac{2+\sqrt3}{(2-\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt3)}\\\tan\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)&=2+\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB&=180^\circ-30^\circ-\theta\\\angle ACB&=150^\circ-\theta.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Use the triangle angle sum before applying a compound-angle identity.

answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin(150^\circ-\theta)}{3+3\sqrt{3}}&=\frac{\sin\theta}{3}\\\sin(150^\circ-\theta)&=\frac{3+3\sqrt{3}}{3}\sin\theta\\\sin(150^\circ-\theta)&=(1+\sqrt{3})\sin\theta.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Use the sine rule with AB opposite angle C and AC opposite θ.

answer.worked:
Using the sine-difference expansion in part (b),
$$\begin{align*}\sin150^\circ\cos\theta-\cos150^\circ\sin\theta&=(1+\sqrt{3})\sin\theta\\\frac12\cos\theta+\frac{\sqrt{3}}2\sin\theta&=(1+\sqrt{3})\sin\theta\\\cos\theta&=(2+\sqrt{3})\sin\theta\\\tan\theta&=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}\\\tan\theta&=2-\sqrt{3}.\end{align*}$$
Also,
$$\begin{align*}\tan15^\circ&=\tan(45^\circ-30^\circ)\\\tan15^\circ&=\frac{1-1/\sqrt{3}}{1+1/\sqrt{3}}\\\tan15^\circ&=2-\sqrt{3}.\end{align*}$$
Since $0<\theta<90^\circ$, $\theta=15^\circ$.
